Na.history: Sodium compounds such as salt and *natron* (natural sodium carbonate, used by Egyptians for mummification) have been used for thousands of years. The metal was first isolated in **1807 by Humphry Davy** at the Royal Institution in London. He passed a current from a large voltaic pile through molten caustic soda (NaOH), only days after isolating potassium the same way. Davy named it from *soda*. The symbol **Na** comes from the Latin *natrium*, after natron.
Na.production:
Sodium metal is made in the **Downs cell** (1924) by electrolysing molten sodium chloride at about 600 °C. Calcium chloride is added to lower the melting point from 801 °C. Liquid sodium collects at the iron cathode and chlorine gas at the graphite anode. Sodium **compounds** matter far more than the metal. Salt (NaCl) is mined or evaporated from seawater. Sodium hydroxide comes from the chlor-alkali process, and sodium carbonate from the Solvay process or the mineral trona.

The metal is used to make titanium and other reactive metals, as a heat-transfer liquid in fast nuclear reactors, and in organic synthesis. Low-pressure **sodium-vapour lamps** give the orange glow of old street lights, which is almost pure 589 nm light.
Na.chemistry: Sodium is a soft metal that can be cut with a knife, revealing a shiny surface that tarnishes within seconds. It is stored under oil. Its single 3s electron is easily lost (first ionization energy 496 kJ/mol), so sodium is almost always found as Na⁺. When it burns it forms mainly sodium **peroxide**, Na₂O₂, rather than the simple oxide. Na⁺ ions carry nerve impulses, and our cells constantly pump them out with the sodium–potassium pump.

reactions.note: Sodium floats, melts into a ball, and skates across the water; the hydrogen may ignite with a yellow flame.
A classic demonstration: molten sodium burns in chlorine to make table salt.
Burning in air gives mainly the peroxide.
Electrolysis of molten salt in the Downs cell.

reactions.eq: NaCl + NH₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → NaHCO₃ + NH₄Cl
reactions.note: The key step of the Solvay process for washing soda.

Na.safety: Sodium reacts violently with water, producing hydrogen that can explode and corrosive sodium hydroxide that burns skin and eyes. It must be handled with dry tools and stored under mineral oil. Sodium fires need dry sand or a class D extinguisher, never water.

Mg.history: In 1618 a farmer called Henry Wicker found that cows refused to drink from a bitter well at **Epsom**, England. The water contained magnesium sulfate, later sold as ‘Epsom salts’. **Joseph Black** showed in 1755 that *magnesia* (magnesium oxide) was different from lime. **Humphry Davy** isolated a small amount of impure metal in 1808 by electrolysis, and **Antoine Bussy** made it in a purer form in 1831 by reducing magnesium chloride with potassium. The name comes from Magnesia, a district of Thessaly in Greece.
Mg.production:
China produces about 85 % of the world’s magnesium using the **Pidgeon process**. Calcined dolomite (MgO·CaO) is heated with ferrosilicon at about 1200 °C under vacuum, and magnesium vapour distils off and condenses: 2MgO + Si → 2Mg + SiO₂. The alternative is **electrolysis of molten MgCl₂**, made from seawater or salt-lake brines. This is the Dow process, first used in 1916; seawater holds about 1.3 g of magnesium per litre.

Magnesium is the lightest structural metal (two-thirds the density of aluminium). It is used in alloys for car parts, laptop and camera bodies, and aircraft, and added to aluminium for drinks cans. It is also used to remove sulfur from steel, in flares and fireworks, and as **Grignard reagents** (RMgX) in organic synthesis.
Mg.chemistry: Magnesium is a reactive group 2 metal, protected by a thin oxide layer. It reacts slowly with cold water, quickly with steam, and readily with acids. Burning magnesium is hot enough to keep burning in **carbon dioxide** and even in nitrogen. Mg²⁺ is essential for life: it sits at the centre of every **chlorophyll** molecule, and hundreds of enzymes need it, including all those that use ATP.

reactions.note: Burns with a dazzling white light. Never look directly at it.
Vigorous fizzing: a standard rates-of-reaction experiment.
With steam; with cold water the reaction is very slow and gives Mg(OH)₂.
Burning magnesium keeps burning in carbon dioxide, leaving black specks of carbon.
Some magnesium nitride forms when magnesium burns in air.

Mg.safety: Solid magnesium is safe to handle, but powder, ribbon and swarf are flammable. A magnesium fire burns at about 3000 °C. **Water makes it worse** (steam gives hydrogen), and so does CO₂, so use dry sand or a class D extinguisher. Do not look at burning magnesium: the UV-rich light can damage the eyes.

Al.history:
Alum, a double sulfate of aluminium, was used in ancient times for dyeing and medicine. Humphry Davy proposed the element in 1808 and gave it names that became ‘aluminum’ (US) and ‘aluminium’ (UK and IUPAC). **Hans Christian Ørsted** made the first impure aluminium in **1825**, and **Friedrich Wöhler** improved the method in 1827. In the 1850s Henri Sainte-Claire Deville produced it by reducing aluminium chloride with sodium. It was still so expensive that Napoleon III served his most honoured guests with aluminium cutlery, and a small aluminium pyramid was placed on top of the Washington Monument in 1884.

In **1886 Charles Martin Hall** (USA) and **Paul Héroult** (France), both 22 years old, independently invented the electrolytic process still used today. Together with Carl Josef Bayer’s 1888 process for purifying bauxite, it made aluminium cheap.
Al.production:
**Bauxite** ore (mostly Al(OH)₃ and AlO(OH)) is mined in Australia, Guinea, China and Brazil. In the **Bayer process** it is dissolved in hot sodium hydroxide, which leaves behind ‘red mud’ (iron oxides). Pure aluminium hydroxide is precipitated and heated to alumina (Al₂O₃). In the **Hall–Héroult process** the alumina is dissolved in molten **cryolite** (Na₃AlF₆) at about 960 °C, far below alumina’s 2072 °C melting point, and electrolysed. The carbon anodes slowly burn away to CO₂.

The process uses about 13–15 kWh of electricity per kilogram, so smelters are built near cheap power. **Recycling** aluminium needs only about 5 % of that energy. Aluminium is used in transport, packaging (cans, foil), construction, power lines and cookware.
Al.chemistry: Aluminium is the **most abundant metal in Earth’s crust** (about 8 %). It is very reactive (E° = −1.66 V), but an invisible, tough oxide layer only a few nanometres thick protects it from corrosion. **Anodising** thickens this layer and allows it to be dyed. Aluminium oxide and hydroxide are **amphoteric**: they dissolve in both acids and strong bases. Its compounds include corundum, which with traces of chromium is ruby and with iron and titanium is sapphire.

reactions.note: The thermite reaction: hot enough to melt the iron it makes.
Slow to start until the oxide film is dissolved.
Amphoteric: aluminium also dissolves in strong alkali (one reason drain cleaners fizz with foil).
Overall electrolysis in the Hall–Héroult cell; the oxygen reacts with the carbon anodes.
Aluminium hydroxide is used as an antacid.

Al.safety: Bulk aluminium is safe. Fine aluminium **powder** is flammable and can explode as a dust cloud, which is why it is used in fireworks and solid rocket fuel. In the past, aluminium in dialysis fluids harmed kidney patients. Studies have not confirmed a link with Alzheimer’s disease.

Si.history:
In 1787 Lavoisier suspected that silica (quartz) was the oxide of an unknown element. **Joseph Gay-Lussac** and **Louis Thénard** probably made impure silicon in 1811, but **Jöns Jacob Berzelius** is credited with isolating it in **1823**, by heating potassium fluorosilicate with potassium. The name comes from the Latin *silex*, flint. In 1817 the Scottish chemist Thomas Thomson gave it the ending *-on* to match boron and carbon, because it is a non-metal.

The first silicon transistor was made in 1954. The industry built on it gave **Silicon Valley** its name.
Si.production:
**Metallurgical-grade silicon** (about 98–99 % pure) is made by reducing quartz with carbon in an electric arc furnace at around 2000 °C: SiO₂ + 2C → Si + 2CO. China produces most of it. It is used mainly in aluminium alloys and to make silicones.

For electronics and solar cells silicon must be **99.9999999 %** pure or better. In the **Siemens process** silicon reacts with HCl to give trichlorosilane (SiHCl₃), which is purified by distillation and decomposed on hot silicon rods. Single crystals for computer chips are grown by the **Czochralski method**, slowly pulling a seed crystal out of molten silicon, and then sliced into wafers.
Si.chemistry: Silicon is the **second most abundant element in Earth’s crust** (about 28 %). It is always found combined with oxygen, in **silicates** built from SiO₄ tetrahedra, which make up most rocks, clays and sand. Elemental silicon is a shiny grey **metalloid** and a **semiconductor**, with a band gap of 1.1 eV and the same crystal structure as diamond. Unlike carbon, silicon does not form stable double bonds. That is why CO₂ is a gas made of small molecules, while SiO₂ is a hard 3D network solid.

reactions.note: Carbothermal reduction in an electric arc furnace.
The first step of the Siemens purification process.
Silica dissolves in hot concentrated alkali, forming ‘water glass’.
Silicon tetrachloride hydrolyses violently in moist air.
Thermal oxidation grows the insulating oxide layers in microchips.

Si.safety: Elemental silicon and amorphous silica have low toxicity. Breathing **crystalline silica dust** (from stone cutting, sandblasting, engineered countertops) causes **silicosis** and lung cancer. Silane (SiH₄) gas ignites spontaneously in air.

P.history:
Phosphorus was the first element discovered by a known person by a documented method. In **1669** the Hamburg alchemist **Hennig Brand**, searching for the philosopher’s stone, boiled down a huge quantity of human urine and heated the residue strongly. He collected a white, waxy substance that **glowed in the dark** and burst into flame in air. He named it from the Greek *phosphoros*, ‘light-bearer’. In 1769 Johan Gottlieb Gahn and Carl Wilhelm Scheele showed that bones contain phosphorus, a much better source.

White phosphorus matches poisoned many factory workers with ‘**phossy jaw**’, a bone-destroying disease. The London matchgirls’ strike of 1888 helped lead to its ban. Safety matches use red phosphorus, on the striking strip instead of the match head.
P.production:
Phosphorus comes from **phosphate rock** (apatite, Ca₅(PO₄)₃F). **Morocco** holds about 70 % of known reserves, and China and the USA are also big producers. Over 90 % of phosphate rock is treated with sulfuric acid to make **phosphoric acid** and fertilisers. Elemental white phosphorus is made by heating phosphate rock with silica and coke in an electric furnace at about 1500 °C. The phosphorus vapour is condensed under water.

Phosphorus is a **non-renewable** resource that crops cannot grow without. Its runoff from fields and sewage feeds algal blooms (eutrophication) in rivers and lakes.
P.chemistry: Phosphorus has several **allotropes**. **White phosphorus** is made of P₄ tetrahedra: very reactive, toxic, it ignites in air at about 30 °C and glows faintly as it slowly oxidises (chemiluminescence). **Red phosphorus** is a polymer and much more stable. **Black phosphorus** has layers like graphite. Phosphorus shows oxidation states from −3 to +5. Phosphate is central to life: it forms the backbone of DNA and RNA, stores energy as ATP, and builds bones and teeth as hydroxyapatite.

reactions.note: White phosphorus burns with a bright flame and dense white smoke.
Phosphorus pentoxide is an extremely effective drying agent; with water it gives phosphoric acid.
Electric-furnace production of white phosphorus.
Making ‘superphosphate’ fertiliser.
Phosphorus trichloride is made for pesticides and flame retardants; excess chlorine gives PCl₅.

P.safety: **White phosphorus is very toxic** (a fraction of a gram can kill) and catches fire on its own in air, causing deep, slow-healing burns. It is stored under water. It is used in incendiary weapons, which international law restricts. Red phosphorus is far safer but still flammable. Many organophosphorus compounds are pesticides or nerve agents.

S.history: Sulfur has been known since ancient times as ‘**brimstone**’ (burning stone). It occurs as yellow crystals near volcanoes and hot springs. Homer’s *Odyssey* mentions burning it to purify a house, and Chinese alchemists of the 9th century mixed it with saltpetre and charcoal to make **gunpowder**. Lavoisier recognised it as an element in 1777. The spelling ‘sulfur’ became the IUPAC standard in 1990.
S.production:
In the 19th century most sulfur came from mines in **Sicily**, worked in terrible conditions. From 1894 the **Frasch process** pumped superheated water into underground deposits in Louisiana and Texas, melting the sulfur and forcing it to the surface. Today almost all sulfur is a **by-product of cleaning natural gas and crude oil**. Poisonous hydrogen sulfide is converted to sulfur in the **Claus process**.

About 85 % of sulfur is turned into **sulfuric acid** by the Contact process. It is the world’s most produced industrial chemical, used for fertilisers, metal processing, batteries and countless other products. Sulfur is also used to vulcanise rubber (Charles Goodyear, 1839), and in fungicides and matches.
S.chemistry: Elemental sulfur consists of crown-shaped **S₈ rings**. It has many allotropes: rhombic sulfur is stable at room temperature, monoclinic sulfur forms above 95 °C, and quickly cooling molten sulfur gives rubbery ‘plastic sulfur’. Sulfur shows oxidation states from −2 (sulfides, H₂S) to +6 (sulfates). In living things, the **disulfide bridges** between cysteine residues help hold proteins in shape. Sulfur dioxide from burning fossil fuels causes **acid rain**.

reactions.note: Burns with a pale-blue flame.
Contact process: V₂O₅ catalyst, about 450 °C, 1–2 atm.
SO₃ is absorbed into sulfuric acid first, because adding it straight to water makes an uncontrollable acid mist.
The Claus process recovers sulfur from natural gas.
A classic demonstration: once started, the mixture glows as the compound forms (unlike a mixture, the product isn’t magnetic).

S.safety: Elemental sulfur has low toxicity but is combustible, and its dust can explode. Burning it gives **sulfur dioxide**, a choking gas that triggers asthma. **Hydrogen sulfide** (rotten-egg smell) is nearly as toxic as hydrogen cyanide. Above about 100 ppm it paralyses the sense of smell, so the warning disappears, and a few breaths at around 1000 ppm can kill.

Cl.history:
In **1774 Carl Wilhelm Scheele** heated the mineral pyrolusite (MnO₂) with hydrochloric acid and obtained a suffocating yellow-green gas that bleached litmus and plant leaves. He and others thought it contained oxygen (‘oxymuriatic acid’). In **1810 Humphry Davy** proved that it is an element and named it after the Greek *chloros*, pale yellow-green.

Chlorine soon transformed daily life. Claude Berthollet developed bleaching with it in 1785, and chlorinating drinking water (from 1908 in Jersey City, USA) caused a dramatic fall in typhoid and cholera. It was also the first major **chemical weapon**: German forces released 168 tonnes of chlorine at Ypres on 22 April 1915.
Cl.production:
Chlorine is made by the **chlor-alkali process**: electrolysis of concentrated brine (sodium chloride solution). Chlorine forms at the anode, and hydrogen and sodium hydroxide at the cathode. Modern plants use an ion-exchange **membrane** to keep the products apart. The older mercury cells, which released mercury into the environment, have been phased out in most countries. Over 70 million tonnes are made each year.

About a third becomes **PVC** plastic. Other uses include disinfecting water, bleach, hydrochloric acid, solvents, refining titanium, and making many pharmaceuticals and pesticides.
Cl.chemistry: Chlorine is a strong oxidising agent and has the **highest electron affinity** of all elements (349 kJ/mol), slightly above fluorine’s. It shows oxidation states from −1 (chloride) to +7 (perchlorate, ClO₄⁻). In water and alkali it **disproportionates**: part is reduced to chloride and part oxidised to hypochlorite or chlorate. Chloride ions are the main negative ions in body fluids, and stomach acid is hydrochloric acid.

reactions.note: The chlor-alkali process.
Cold dilute alkali: making household bleach (sodium hypochlorite).
Hot alkali gives chlorate instead.
Chlorine water; hypochlorous acid is the disinfecting agent.
Scheele’s original method, still a laboratory preparation.
Hot iron wool burns in chlorine, giving brown iron(III) chloride.

Cl.safety: Chlorine gas is **toxic**. In the moist lining of the lungs it forms acids that cause fluid build-up (pulmonary oedema). It can be smelt at under 1 ppm, and concentrations above about 30 ppm are dangerous. **Never mix bleach with acids** (toilet cleaners, vinegar), which releases chlorine, **or with ammonia**, which gives toxic chloramines.

Ar.history: In 1785 Henry Cavendish noticed that a small bubble of air, about 1/120 of it, could not be made to react, no matter how long he sparked it with oxygen. A century later **Lord Rayleigh** found that nitrogen taken from the air was about 0.5 % denser than nitrogen made from ammonia. In **1894** he and **William Ramsay** removed all the nitrogen from air by passing it over hot magnesium. They were left with a gas that had new spectral lines and would not react with anything. They named it after the Greek *argos*, ‘lazy’. The discovery added a whole new group to the periodic table, and both men received Nobel Prizes in 1904.
Ar.production: Argon is 0.934 % of the atmosphere, the **third most abundant gas** in air and almost 30 times more abundant than CO₂. It is collected cheaply as a by-product of air-separation plants. It is used as a **shielding gas** for welding (MIG/TIG) and for growing silicon crystals. It also fills incandescent and fluorescent lamps and double-glazed windows (it conducts heat poorly), and is used in argon-oxygen decarburisation for stainless steel, in argon-ion lasers, and to preserve wine.
Ar.chemistry: Argon has a full outer shell (3s²3p⁶) and forms no stable compounds under normal conditions. The only known neutral compound is **argon fluorohydride**, HArF, made in 2000 at the University of Helsinki. It exists only below about 27 K, frozen in a solid argon matrix. Almost all of Earth’s argon is argon-40, made by the radioactive decay of potassium-40 in rocks. This decay is the basis of **potassium–argon dating** of volcanic rocks.

reactions.note: Electron capture by potassium-40 (half-life 1.25 billion years) produces argon, used in K–Ar dating.

reactions.eq: Ar + HF → HArF (at < 27 K, UV light)
reactions.note: The only known neutral argon compound; it falls apart again when warmed.

Ar.safety: Argon is non-toxic, but it is **denser than air** and collects in low places such as pits, tanks and basements. It displaces oxygen there without any warning signs. Liquid argon (−186 °C) causes cold burns.
